There is a long road between the conception of an anime to the time it airs on television. This path is fraught with obstacles, big and small. It can be an extremely rewarding, as well as incredibly punishing experience. Shirobako relates the perilous journey of anime production with beauty and a deftness that is hard to come by in any medium.

Shirobako tells the story of Aoi Miyamori as she works to produce anime at Musashino Animation. Alongside her is a cast of vivacious characters, from fellow production assistants to key animators to voice actors, and so on. Shirobako aims to emulate the winding road of anime production to its viewers, which includes the innumerable victories and defeats that occur every moment of a single production. The series certainly achieves this goal, though it sometimes gets lost in the technical details and jargon of the industry. Despite this downfall, Shirobako still manages to convey the general idea of what's going on to the viewer, and much can be learned about the anime industry from this show. But learning about anime production is only one facet of this show. Where Shirobako really shines is in its use of conflict in order to channel the intense emotions that are involved in devoting oneself to a project. Many times throughout the series, I found myself about to pull my own hair out on behalf of Aoi and the rest of the cast. It was the use of these moments that also led to me cursing when things fell apart or cheering when pulled through. Truly, Shirobako wraps the viewer around its finger and doesn't let go.

In addition to the delicate use of conflict to keep the viewer wanting for more, the large set of characters in Shirobako are largely well-developed. The only downside to such a large cast is that it's very easy to lose track of who is who. Even at the end of the show, there were some characters who I did not remember. However, Shirobako does have a core few characters that the viewer will undoubtedly grow attached to. These few characters are very well-realized, with their own motivations, backstories, and personalities, all of which drive them to interact with each other and their work in convincing ways. You have slackers and hardworkers, along with dreamers and those beat down by the reality of the business. In this way, anime production is like any other job, and it is easy to relate to the frustration that all of the characters feel at one point or another.

Shirobako is by no means perfect, but it is definitively top-tier. Its use of conflict and deep characters (many of which are based on actual people in the anime industry) make it a very robust anime that is accessible to anyone -- from people who know every inch of anime production to those that know nothing about it. Although the show can get complicated if you don't completely know what's happening, it never leaves its viewers in the dust. You may not understand everything, but you'll understand what matters. So, have a seat, pick your best girl, and enjoy the ride. Shirobako will not disappoint.
